title: Passive spectral-admittance bounds and exact continuum certificates for multiresonator quantum-memory interfaces
abstract: Broadband quantum-memory interfaces are often assessed by center-frequency impedance matching or by a sampled efficiency curve. Neither supplies an operational continuous-band certificate, and absorption is not automatically reversible storage. We model a passive one-port multiresonator interface by a positive-real spectral admittance with explicitly identified controlled output channels. If their one-photon subspace is mapped isometrically into long-lived registers, the write probability for a normalized spectrum $f$ supported in a band $\mathcal{B}$ is $1-\int_{\mathcal{B}} |r(iω)|^2 |f(ω)|^2\,dω$, and the worst-case write efficiency is $1-\|r\|_{L^\infty(\mathcal{B})}^2$. We prove that a finite passive rational interface cannot have zero reflection on a nonzero interval and derive the Bode--Fano floor $\|r\|_\infty \geq \exp[-πκ/(2B)]$ for a band of half-width $B$. At fixed pole locations, minimax synthesis is a quasiconvex semi-infinite problem in the oscillator strengths. We then give an exact computer-assisted certificate: after a decimal design is converted into an explicit rational system, the continuum reflection bound becomes positivity of one univariate polynomial and is proved by Sturm root counting; exact Routh--Hurwitz determinants certify stability and minimum phase. In units $κ=2$ and $B=1$, an 11-mode design obeys $0.064112405 \leq \|r\|_\infty < 0.0641125$, implying a conditional uniform write guarantee above $0.995889587$. This is a reproducible certificate for a specified interface, not a claim of global movable-pole optimality or of an experimentally complete memory.
summary: This theoretical paper develops a rigorous framework to certify the broadband write efficiency of passive quantum memory interfaces. It moves beyond simple peak measurements by deriving fundamental spectral bounds (Bode–Fano floor) and providing exact mathematical certificates based on polynomial positivity for specific multi-mode designs. This work establishes quantitative, verifiable performance guarantees essential for building reliable quantum hardware.
main_problem: The paper addresses the need for a rigorous, continuous-band certificate to quantify the write efficiency of broadband quantum memory interfaces, moving beyond simple peak measurements.
main_result: It derives the Bode–Fano floor bound for passive interfaces and provides an exact, computer-assisted certificate showing that specific multi-mode designs achieve high conditional uniform write guarantees (e.g., >0.9958).
method: The analysis uses positive-real spectral admittance modeling, relating write probability to the minimum reflection magnitude $\|r\|_{\infty}$ over the operational band.
model_or_system: The system is a passive one-port multiresonator interface modeled by a positive-real spectral admittance $\Sigma(s)$, which couples an input field to internal long-lived quantum memory registers.
key_observables: Worst-case write efficiency ($\eta_{wc}^w$), reflection amplitude $|r(i\omega)|$, and the minimum achievable $\|r\|_{\infty}$ over a specified band $\mathcal{B}$.
important_parameters: The spectral bandwidth $B$ and coupling parameter $\kappa$; the specific number of resonant modes (e.g., 11-mode design).
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes passive, stationary elements and focuses on rationalized designs to derive exact certificates; global optimality over all pole placements remains an open question.
figures_summary: Figure 2 illustrates the spectral flattening of the reflection magnitude $|r(i\omega)|$ as the number of controlled modes increases. Figure 4 shows Monte Carlo sensitivity analysis for the write efficiency.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from defining the operational deficiency (reflection defect) to deriving theoretical bounds (Bode–Fano floor), establishing convexity conditions for synthesis, and finally providing exact verification methods using polynomial positivity checks (Sturm root counting).
why_interesting: This work provides essential mathematical tools—exact certificates and rigorous lower bounds—for quantifying the performance limits of quantum hardware components like quantum memories, which is crucial for scaling up photonic quantum information processing.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. Operational qualification of the passive interface. The rational admittance fixes scattering from the signal port into controlled output fields. Reflection defect becomes memory-write probability only after a coherent isometry maps the admitted controlled-field subspace into a long-lived register; dashed channels represent uncontrolled loss and do not count as storage.
FIG. 2. Reflection magnitude for four passive symmetric candidates. Vertical dotted lines mark the design band. The spectra flatten as the number of controlled internal modes increases.

FIG. 3. Positive-frequency half of the 11-mode reflection spectrum. The dashed line is the exact continuum upper bound. Markers show numerically resolved ripple maxima; they are diagnostics, whereas the bound is proved by exact polynomial arithmetic.

FIG. 4. Reproducible Monte Carlo sensitivity of the nominal 11-mode candidate under independent mean-preserving log- normal perturbations. Solid markers show the median and 95th percentile of the dense-grid maximum. These statistics are model-dependent diagnostics, not deterministic guarantees.

Figure 4 shows a separate, fully reproducible Monte Carlo sensitivity study. Every positive 11-mode param- eter is perturbed independently according to the mean- preserving log-normal model p′ = p exp(σZ −σ2/2) with Z ∼N(0, 1); 1200 samples per spread, a 12001-point grid on [0, 1], and seed 20260711 are used. This is not a confidence statement about any fabrication process unless that distribution is experimentally justified. Its purpose is diagnostic: the nominal minimax design is sharp, and robust synthesis or postfabrication retuning is likely to be important.
